SCHOOL GARDEN · GARDEN FLOWERS

Garden Flowers

Age 2 YearsSubject Nature & TalkClass School GardenDuration 3–5 minutes

Big yellow sunflowers, roses, tulips and bluebells — the flower bed is full of names waiting to be learned. Twelve bright blooms, one big picture at a time.

Nothing to prepare and nothing to read. You say the flower name, your toddler points, sniffs the air or giggles — a moment on a card counts, and the real garden can wait for your next walk.

TOGETHER · WHERE FLOWERS GROW

Where flowers grow.

Flowers turn up in the most ordinary places — here is where to look, gently and without picking.

  • Sunflower

    “In gardens and on farms, standing taller than you by summer.”

  • Daisy

    “Right in the grass — little white stars on any lawn.”

  • Lavender

    “In purple rows in gardens; bees visit it all day long.”

  • Lotus

    “On warm, still ponds — floating on a big green pad.”

  • Bluebell

    “In woods in spring, ringing blue under the trees.”

  • Rose

    “In rose beds and parks — smell first, touch very gently if a grown-up says it is okay.”

SOLVE THE SHEETS — ON PAPER OR ON SCREEN

Solve the garden flower cards together.

The twelve flower cards print two to a page, straight from your browser. Printed, cut and named, they are the collection’s real worksheets — and on screen, every card page can be drawn on directly.

  1. 01

    Print the cards

    Open the printable cards and print all twelve, two to a page. Cut them out together, saying each flower’s name.

  2. 02

    Name the colors

    Say each flower’s color as you name it — a pink flower, a yellow flower. Colors hide inside this collection for free.

  3. 03

    Smell around you

    Flowers are the smell-it collection: on the next walk, sniff (gently!) one real flower and name its card.

  4. 04

    Draw a flower

    Pick a favourite card and draw the flower on paper — or on its card page with the Write & Color layer.

Open the printable sheets ↗Draw on the cards on screen ↗

Every card page has a Write & Color layer: your child can draw right on the card with a finger, a stylus or the mouse, then save the finished work. Nothing is uploaded anywhere.

TAKE IT OFF SCREEN

A look-and-smell flower hunt.

Take the names outside — or to a window box, a park or a bunch of flowers at home. Flowers are for looking at and smelling, not picking.

Try one today

  • Spot a flower on your walk and say its colour together.
  • Smell a rose or a herb together — snif, snif, what does it smell like?
  • Count the petals on a daisy — one, two, three… as far as your toddler goes.
  • Find a bee visiting a flower and watch it quietly — the bee is working.
  • Point at every yellow flower you can find, then try pink.

Flowers stay on the plant — picking is for grown-ups. One flower noticed and named together is a complete hunt, and a grown-up stays close the whole time.

A NOTE FROM THE PRINCIPAL

For the grown-ups.

Your toddler does not need every flower name to stick. Big, bright pictures and your voice are doing the teaching — the words ride along, and one favourite flower repeated happily is a complete lesson.

TIPS FOR PARENTS

Tips for Parents

Colours before names. Yellow! Pink! Purple! — a colour shouted happily is already flower learning.

Add the senses: reach tall like a sunflower, sniff like a rose, ding like a bluebell. Movement sticks the words.

Flowers stay on the plant. Looking and smelling is the game; picking is for grown-ups with a reason.

Age ranges are a guide. Go at your child’s pace.

    LEARNING PATH LESSON · GARDEN FLOWERS · AGES 2 YEARS

    Sunflower — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

    This lesson grows a giant on your rug: your toddler reaches up like a sunflower, hunts for yellow on the way to the shops, and hears where sunflower seeds come from.

    What is this?

    A sunflower is a very tall flower with a big round face and bright yellow petals all around it. It turns through the day to follow the sun, and its middle is full of seeds.

    What does it mean?

    The sunflower is the set’s standing-stretch card — everything about it points up. For a two-year-old, big-and-yellow is an easy win, and the seed story quietly plants the idea that flowers come from tiny things.

    What does the child need to know?

    Sunflowers are tall, yellow and full of seeds; birds and people both eat them. We look at the big face, we stretch up beside it, and if we ever grow one at home it will need a whole summer of watering.

    Why this matters

    Reaching tall is real exercise — balance, stretch, wobble, hold — and yellow is usually one of the first colours a toddler names. The sunflower hands you both in one bright card.

    What it teaches

    Whole-body stretching and balance, colour naming (yellow above all), size words (tall, taller, giant), early seed-to-plant thinking, and pointing practice on a big, unmissable target.

    Words to learn

    sunflowertallyellowpetalsseedsgrow

    Say this to your child

    “"Look at the sunflower! It is so tall and so yellow — the tallest friend in the whole garden. Can you stretch up tall like a sunflower? Up, up, up! Its big face follows the sun all day, and hidden in the middle are seeds — seeds that grow brand-new sunflowers."”

    Step by step

    1. Show the card and say sunflower in three beats — sun-flow-er — then hold your hand way up high to show how tall this friend stands.
    2. Stretch together: up on tippy toes, arms high, wobbling like a tall flower in the breeze, then flop down and do it again.
    3. Ask where the petals are and where the big round face is — let one finger do the finding while you name each part.
    4. Tell the seed story: the sunflower’s middle is packed with seeds, and every seed can grow a whole new sunflower next summer.
    5. Take yellow hunting on your next walk — count the yellow things you find together and cheer the loudest one like a tiny sunflower fan.

    Look closer at the picture

    Hold the card low and let your toddler find the flower with one finger. Say sunflower together, then reach both hands to the ceiling — this friend is the tall one, and the stretch is the point.

    Ask your child

    "Is the sunflower big or little?" "Can you stretch up tall?" "What colour is the sunflower?" "What is hiding in the middle?" — answered with a stretch, a proud "yellow!" and a finger pressed on the seeds.

    What your child can say or do

    "Sun-flow-er!" Expect tall-walking past every fence, yellow shouted at buses and bananas, and seeds requested at snack time. "Taller than a sunflower yet?" may become your family’s measuring joke.

    Out in the real world

    Sunflowers tower over gardens, allotments and farm-shop doorways all summer. Every roadside giant is a rerun — point, stretch, name the yellow — and a packet of seeds makes the lesson plantable at home.

    Try it together

    Grow like a sunflower: crouch as a tiny seed on the floor, then rise slowly while you tell the story — a little sprout, a stem, higher, higher — until your sunflower stands at full stretch, arms wide as petals.

    Understanding check

    Next time you pass something tall and yellow, listen: an unprompted "sunflower!" means the word has roots. A standing stretch on request seals the lesson.

    Parent tips

    Keep the stretch game near nap time in reverse — big movements first, then flop and rest like a sunflower at dusk. If you plant real seeds, put the pot where your toddler waters it daily; the waiting is the lesson.

    Staying safe

    Stretching happens on clear floor, away from furniture corners and radiator edges. If you grow sunflowers, the watering is toddler work but the planting soil stays out of mouths — hands get washed after every gardening session.

    This lesson pairs with the Sunflower flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Garden Flowers (School Garden).

    Rose — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

    This lesson gives your toddler the garden’s best smell word: sniff the pretend rose, sniff the kitchen, sniff the outside air — and learn why we smell roses with our noses only.

    What is this?

    A rose is a flower with layers and layers of soft petals and a scent that makes everyone lean in. Rose bushes grow prickles — sharp little spikes — on their stems.

    What does it mean?

    The rose teaches smelling as a way of knowing. Toddlers live nose-first anyway, so a flower that asks for a sniff is the most natural lesson in the set — with a visible reason (prickles!) for careful hands.

    What does the child need to know?

    Roses smell lovely and their petals feel soft — but the stems carry prickles, so we sniff with our noses and keep our fingers to ourselves. Grown-ups hold the smelling when the rose is close.

    Why this matters

    A flower with a boundary built in is a gift: your toddler practises the ask-first, touch-later pattern on something they meet everywhere. And sniffing games sharpen a sense most cards ignore.

    What it teaches

    Smell awareness and the sniffing motion itself, gentle-breath control, soft/hard and smooth/prickly contrast words, and the early safety habit of looking before reaching.

    Words to learn

    rosesmellsniffpetalspricklessoft

    Say this to your child

    “"A rose! Sniff, sniff — roses smell so lovely. Soft petals, layer after layer. But look here: prickles on the stem! So our noses do the smelling and our hands stay down. When you want a really big sniff of a real rose, you come to me first and we sniff together."”

    Step by step

    1. Show the card, say rose, and take a big theatrical sniff of the air — the smell should arrive before the explanation does.
    2. Sniff-hunt the room together: what smells nice here? An orange, a hand cream, the outside air through the door — sniff and give each one a word.
    3. Hold your palm flat and stroke it with one finger: petals are soft like this — then tap your other arm lightly: prickles! Soft and spiky, felt in the air.
    4. Say the rule with your hands: noses smell the rose, fingers stay far away, and smelling close happens only in a grown-up’s arms.
    5. Finish with a pretend bouquet — sniff each invisible rose you hand each other and sigh happily, three stems at least.

    Look closer at the picture

    Say rose and sniff the air beside the card, eyes closed — then ask your toddler to find the petals with one careful finger. The flower on the card does the smelling for you today.

    Ask your child

    "What does the rose smell like?" "Can you sniff like a puppy?" "Are the petals soft or spiky?" "Who holds you when you smell a real rose?" — answered with a sniff, a soft word and a hug-shaped answer.

    What your child can say or do

    "Sniff sniff!" Expect dramatic sniffing at fruit, flowers and strangers’ perfume, roses declared on every walk, and the prickle rule recited at bushes. Random sighs of "lovely!" are part of the course.

    Out in the real world

    Roses bloom in gardens, parks and petrol-station tubs all summer, and appear in every bunch at the shop. Each one is a sniffing station: stop, sniff the air from a step away, name the flower.

    Try it together

    Smell detective: set out three safe smells — orange peel, a herb, a flower — sniff each with closed eyes, and name them. Then add the pretend rose and let your toddler teach YOU which is which.

    Understanding check

    Watch the next rose encounter: if your toddler sniffs the air with hands clasped and looks at you for permission to come closer, the prickle rule has bloomed — lesson complete.

    Parent tips

    Keep the sniff pretend whenever the rose is out of arm’s reach — the game works at any distance. Grow a rosemary or mint pot for a smell-my-child-can-pick-safely: same joy, no prickles.

    Staying safe

    Rose prickles scratch, so all close-up smelling happens in your arms or not at all — hands stay down outdoors. Watch that sniffing enthusiasm does not become leaning into flowerbeds: thorns, wasps and nettles live there too.

    This lesson pairs with the Rose flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Garden Flowers (School Garden).

    Tulip — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

    This lesson hands your toddler a shape before a flower: two hands cupped into a tulip, a butterfly coming to drink, and a street full of spring colours to sort afterwards.

    What is this?

    A tulip is a spring flower whose petals close into a cup shape on a tall green stem. Tulips come in many colours and open in the morning light.

    What does it mean?

    The tulip is the set’s shape-flower: cup is a shape your toddler’s hands already know. Naming a flower by what it looks like — a cup on a stem — teaches the best trick in nature-watching: look for the shape.

    What does the child need to know?

    Tulips look like little cups on stems and bloom in spring, in lots of colours. We cup our hands to be one, we count the colours outside, and tulips in a vase close up at night — a tiny surprise worth checking.

    Why this matters

    Shape-first naming is how young children learn to see: cup, star, bell. The tulip also carries spring itself — after a winter of grey, a flower your toddler can spot, name and colour-count is a genuine season marker.

    What it teaches

    Hand shaping (cupping both palms), colour collecting on walks, the spring idea (flowers come back), sipping imitation for pretend play, and early comparison — which tulip is redder, which stem taller.

    Words to learn

    tulipcuppetalsstemspringcolours

    Say this to your child

    “"A tulip! Look — it is shaped like a little cup on a stem. Can you make a tulip with your hands? Cup them up... now I am a butterfly, sip sip! Tulips come in spring, in every colour — let us count the colours we see outside today."”

    Step by step

    1. Show the card, say tulip, and cup your two hands together into a flower shape — hold it out for your toddler to smell.
    2. Be the butterfly: with your tulip-hands waiting, dip a pointing finger in and out, sipping — then swap so your toddler is the tulip and you are the butterfly.
    3. Ask where the petals are on the card and where the stem is — one flower, two parts, both easy to point at.
    4. Say the spring story: tulips wake up when the cold months end, which is why parks turn bright all at once.
    5. On your next walk, collect tulip colours out loud — every bed is a sorting tray of reds, pinks and yellows to name together.

    Look closer at the picture

    Cup your hands into a tulip shape and say the word into the cup. Ask your toddler to find the petals on the card and the long stem below them — the flower and its stem, two finds in one.

    Ask your child

    "What shape is the tulip?" "Can you make a cup with your hands?" "Where is the stem?" "How many colours of tulip can we find today?" — answered with cupped hands, a pointing finger and a colour shouted from the buggy.

    What your child can say or do

    "Tulip cup!" Expect hand-cups offered for sipping at snack time, tulips named from the pram all spring, and colours sorted at every flowerbed. Your toddler may hand you an invisible tulip — smell it and sigh.

    Out in the real world

    Tulips fill parks, roundabouts and window boxes in spring, and buckets of them stand outside flower shops. Each cup of colour is a rerun — name the shape, name the colour, sip like a butterfly and move on.

    Try it together

    Tulip colour hunt: pick one colour before you leave the house, then find that tulip outside — or in a book, or out the window. One colour, one walk, one triumphant point and shout.

    Understanding check

    Say "tulip" cold tomorrow morning: if two hands cup together before any words arrive, the shape and the flower are one — the lesson is in your toddler’s hands now.

    Parent tips

    Keep the cup-hands handy — they double as a whisper-cup for quiet talk. If a vase of tulips lives at home, check them at night together: closed at dark, open by morning is a daily magic worth a gasp.

    Staying safe

    Shop tulips are for looking and sniffing, not chewing — stems and petals stay out of mouths, and vase water is strictly not a drink. On tulip beds, feet stay on the path; flowers look but are not picked.

    This lesson pairs with the Tulip flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Garden Flowers (School Garden).

    LEARNING PATH LESSON · GARDEN FLOWERS · AGES 2 YEARS

    Daisy — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

    This lesson turns every lawn into a hunt: your toddler learns the daisy — small, bright, everywhere — and gets the proudest find in the whole flower set, because they found it themselves.

    What is this?

    A daisy is a small flower that grows low in grass, with a ring of narrow petals around a round gold middle. Daisies open in the morning and close again in the evening.

    What does it mean?

    The daisy is usually the first flower a child finds without help — small enough to be a discovery, common enough to be findable every single day. Independent discovery is the whole prize at two.

    What does the child need to know?

    Daisies are the little stars hiding in the grass, with a gold middle and petals like a collar. We find them with our eyes, we never pick the whole patch, and drawing one — circle, spokes — is daisy practice too.

    Why this matters

    A findable treasure builds watching skills better than any flashcard: eyes down, scanning, spotting. The daisy also opens and closes with the day, a first clock hiding in the grass.

    What it teaches

    Visual scanning and spotting, tiny-motor pointing at small targets, early drawing (a circle with petals around it), morning-evening rhythm words, and the confidence of a find announced.

    Words to learn

    daisysmallgrasspetalsgoldfind

    Say this to your child

    “"A daisy! Small and bright, hiding in the grass. See the gold middle and the white petals all around? Let us go daisy-hunting — eyes down, looking, looking... there! You found one! We look at them where they grow, and we can draw our own at home."”

    Step by step

    1. Show the card, say daisy, and make a tiny circle with your finger and thumb — this flower is the small one in the set.
    2. Draw a daisy in the air: a little gold circle, then petal-strokes all around — your toddler can add the petals with a pointed finger.
    3. Take the hunt outside to any grass: how many daisies can we find? Count them loosely — one, two, lots — and celebrate every find.
    4. Kneel down at one daisy and look properly: the gold middle, the petal collar, the stem hiding in the grass.
    5. Close with the daisy’s secret: at night the petals close up like hands folded, and morning opens them again — check tomorrow if you can.

    Look closer at the picture

    Make a tiny circle with your fingers and say daisy. Ask your toddler to find the gold middle on the card, then the petals around it — small finds, carefully pointed at, are the whole game.

    Ask your child

    "Is the daisy big or little?" "Where does it hide — in the grass or in the trees?" "Can you find one outside?" "What is in the middle, gold or blue?" — answered with a finger-circle, a hunt and a proud stomp-to-spot.

    What your child can say or do

    "Daisy!" Expect lawn-hunting at every stop, daisies pointed out from car seats, and a first drawn flower — one gold circle, petals exploding around it. Daisies may be gifted to you by the fistful. Say thank you.

    Out in the real world

    Daisies grow in every park, lawn, verge and crack with grass — the most findable flower in the world. Each white-and-gold spot is a completed hunt, and no equipment was needed, ever.

    Try it together

    Daisy maths, gently: find one daisy, then another — "one daisy, two daisies!" — and stop while it is still a game. If a grown-up makes a daisy chain, your toddler does the quality control: holding, pointing, approving.

    Understanding check

    On the next lawn, watch before you prompt: eyes-down scanning means the hunt has stuck. A gold-middle point and the word daisy together — lesson fully bloomed.

    Parent tips

    Take the hunt at toddler pace — one daisy is a complete expedition. Keep picking to a single flower in your hand only, and let most daisies stay in the grass: the finding was always the treasure.

    Staying safe

    Lawns hold more than flowers — check the patch for bees, stones and dog mess before the crouching starts. Daisies are not for eating, and newly mown grass, with its sharp little clippings, is a look-only place.

    This lesson pairs with the Daisy flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Garden Flowers (School Garden).

    LEARNING PATH LESSON · GARDEN FLOWERS · AGES 2 YEARS

    Daffodil — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

    This lesson turns a flower into an instrument: your toddler blows a golden trumpet, gathers yellow from every verge, and meets the flower that shows up first, every single year.

    What is this?

    A daffodil is a spring flower shaped like a trumpet on a tall stem, in bright yellow. It blooms in big crowds while the air is still cold, and grows back each year from a bulb hiding underground.

    What does it mean?

    The daffodil is the season’s first headline: colour arrives before the warmth does. For a toddler, a flower that returns every year is a comfortable promise — the world keeps its good things.

    What does the child need to know?

    Daffodils are the yellow trumpets of early spring; they grow from bulbs that sleep underground all winter. We blow our trumpets at them, count them from the path, and leave every trumpet on its stem.

    Why this matters

    The trumpet shape is blowable — and blowing is breath control, the same muscle work behind blowing bubbles and blowing noses. A flower that rewards a toot is a flower a toddler will remember forever.

    What it teaches

    Breath control (the trumpet toot), early-spring seasonal awareness, yellow collecting, counting flower crowds, and the comfort of things that come back — bulbs, birthdays, spring itself.

    Words to learn

    daffodiltrumpetyellowspringbulbblow

    Say this to your child

    “"A daffodil! The golden trumpet of spring. When the cold days end, up pop the daffodils — pa-pa-paaa! Can you blow your trumpet? They grow from little bulbs sleeping under the ground, and they come back every single year. Yellow is their colour — how much yellow can we find today?"”

    Step by step

    1. Show the card, say daffodil, and hold your fist to your mouth like a trumpet — pa-pa-paaa! — blowing the sound out over the card.
    2. Let your toddler toot their own trumpet at the card, then at the window, then at anything yellow you pass today.
    3. Point out the flower’s parts: the trumpet in the middle, the petals standing behind it like a collar, the tall stem holding it up.
    4. Tell the bulb story with a surprise voice: under every daffodil sleeps a little bulb, and when winter ends — pop! — up comes the trumpet.
    5. On your next cold, bright walk, count the daffodils in the parks and verges together — spring is arriving, and your toddler spotted it first.

    Look closer at the picture

    Hold your fist up as a trumpet and say daffodil into it. Ask your toddler to find the trumpet part on the card — the deep cup in the middle — then toot once, gently, at the flower.

    Ask your child

    "What colour is the daffodil?" "Can you blow your trumpet?" "Where does the daffodil sleep before spring?" "How many daffodils can we count today?" — answered with a toot, a "yellow!" and a pointing count from the buggy.

    What your child can say or do

    "Pa-pa-paaa!" Expect trumpet-blowing at every patch of yellow, daffodils announced weeks before they bloom, and bulbs demanded for the garden. Spring may officially begin whenever your toddler says so.

    Out in the real world

    Daffodils line parks, roundabouts, churchyards and roadsides in early spring — the loudest colour of the year. Every golden crowd is a rerun: toot the trumpet, count from the path, walk on warm.

    Try it together

    Trumpet parade: march through the house blowing pretend trumpets, stopping at each yellow thing you pass for a solo — banana, sponge, yellow sock. Daffodil cards get the longest fanfare of all.

    Understanding check

    At the first real daffodil of next spring, watch your toddler’s mouth: if a trumpet rises before any words, the flower and the toot are bonded — the season now has a sound.

    Parent tips

    Buy a pot of growing bulbs in winter and let your toddler water it — watching the bud swell is weeks of free suspense. Keep the toots gentle indoors; trumpets and sleeping babies negotiate through doors.

    Staying safe

    Daffodil bulbs and stems are not for tasting — they can make tummies ill, so bulbs stay stored away and cut flowers stay up high. Trumpet arms need elbow room: toot outdoors or in clear space, never at a sibling’s ear.

    This lesson pairs with the Daffodil flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Garden Flowers (School Garden).

    LEARNING PATH LESSON · GARDEN FLOWERS · AGES 2 YEARS

    Poppy — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

    This lesson is built on the loudest colour in the set: your toddler learns the poppy — red as red can be — then hunts red everywhere and dances one very still flower dance.

    What is this?

    A poppy is a flower with big, thin, papery petals in the brightest red. Poppies like open ground and field edges, and their petals crinkle like tissue paper.

    What does it mean?

    Red is the colour toddlers see first and loudest, and the poppy is red at full volume. The flower also teaches fragility without a single word: petals this thin are for looking, and looking is enough.

    What does the child need to know?

    Poppies are the boldest red flowers, with petals thin as tissue paper. Our eyes do all the looking, we spot red things everywhere once we know the colour, and the petals wobble in the smallest wind.

    Why this matters

    Colour-spotting is a toddler’s first search engine, and red is its best keyword — cars, doors, berries, posts. The poppy hands your child a colour word with a picture attached, and the wind-wobble adds a dance.

    What it teaches

    Colour spotting (red above all), stillness play (be a poppy in the wind), soft-and-thin texture words, field-and-edge place vocabulary, and gentle handling of fragile things — by not handling them.

    Words to learn

    poppyredpetalsfieldpaperywind

    Say this to your child

    “"A poppy! Red, red, red — the brightest flower in the garden. Its petals are thin like paper and they wobble in the wind. Can you stand like a poppy? Still, still... here comes the breeze — wobble, wobble! We look at poppies with our eyes and let the wind do the moving."”

    Step by step

    1. Show the card, say poppy, and open your hand flat and still — the poppy stands its petals wide open too.
    2. Say the colour out loud, twice: red, bright bright red — then ask your toddler to find something red in the room before you move on.
    3. Feel the papery idea with your hands: flutter your fingers like tissue petals, crinkly and light, ready to wobble in the smallest breeze.
    4. Play the poppy dance: stand tall, hold still, then wobble when you blow a little wind at them — flower dancing needs a breeze, and you are the breeze.
    5. End with the rule folded in gently: poppy petals are as thin as paper, so we let them dance where they grow — our eyes do the picking.

    Look closer at the picture

    Open your hand like a wide petal and say poppy. Ask your toddler to point at the flower on the card, then hold a stillness together — two poppies standing in the room — before the wobble begins.

    Ask your child

    "What colour is the poppy?" "Can you find something red in this room?" "Are the petals thick or thin?" "Can you stand still like a poppy?" — answered with a red shout, a finger-point and a beautifully held stillness.

    What your child can say or do

    "Red!" Expect red-spotting from car seats — post boxes, cars, berries — poppies claimed at every field edge, and stillness demanded so the breeze game can begin. The wobble is the part that gets repeated at home.

    Out in the real world

    Poppies blaze along field edges, road verges and any bit of disturbed ground in summer, and they appear on badges and in books. Every flash of field-red is a rerun — point, hold still, wobble together.

    Try it together

    Red hunt: choose red as the day’s colour and keep score out loud on your walk — each find earns a cheer, and the poppy card comes along as the team badge. Back home, sort the red toys into one big pile.

    Understanding check

    Show the card a day later and ask for the colour: an instant "red!" with a finger-petal flutter means the poppy landed. A still-then-wobble on request seals it completely.

    Parent tips

    Keep red-spotting running for a week — the colour needs a whole street to sink in. If the stillness game becomes a favourite, borrow it for waiting rooms: "stand like a poppy" buys you thirty quiet seconds.

    Staying safe

    Poppies grow where the ground is rough — field edges and verges with traffic and stings nearby, so spotting happens from the path. All poppies are look-only: petals this thin tear, and unknown plants stay out of mouths.

    This lesson pairs with the Poppy flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Garden Flowers (School Garden).

    LEARNING PATH LESSON · GARDEN FLOWERS · AGES 2 YEARS

    Lavender — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

    This lesson is the calm one: a slow breath like smelling lavender, a quiet minute watching a busy bush, and the first friendly rule about bees — look at the workers, never touch them.

    What is this?

    Lavender is a bush full of slim purple spikes that smell wonderful, even when dried. Bees love it and visit all summer, buzzing from spike to spike.

    What does it mean?

    Every toddler set needs a slow-down card, and lavender is it. The smell invites one long calm breath — a genuine self-soothing tool — and the bees open the door to watching small creatures work.

    What does the child need to know?

    Lavender smells lovely and stays purple even when dry; bees come to it all day long. We take one slow breath, we watch the bees from a step away, and our hands stay down — the bees are working.

    Why this matters

    One calm breath is the toddler version of a meditation practice, and lavender gives it a smell to hang on. Watching bees teaches focused attention on something tiny, busy and best admired from stillness.

    What it teaches

    Slow-breath control (in through the nose, out long), calm-state practice, colour word (purple), bee awareness with a safe distance built in, and scent memory — smells stick longer than pictures.

    Words to learn

    lavenderpurplesmellbeesbreathcalm

    Say this to your child

    “"Lavender — purple and calm. Can you smell it? Take a slow breath in... and let it out, slow and soft. The bees love this flower too — they buzz all day, working hard. We watch them quietly and keep our hands down. One lavender breath is all we need to feel calm."”

    Step by step

    1. Show the card, say lavender, and take one big slow breath in through your nose, then out even slower — let your toddler hear the calm.
    2. Practise the lavender breath together three times: in like smelling a flower... out like blowing a dandelion. Slow every time.
    3. Point out the spikes on the card — not one big flower but a hundred little ones on one bush.
    4. Tell the bee story softly: bees come to the lavender to work, gathering food, and they like us best when we are still and quiet.
    5. End with a lavender minute: sit by a bush or just breathe slowly together, calm as can be, before the day’s next big feeling arrives.

    Look closer at the picture

    Take one slow, showy breath beside the card and say lavender as you let it out. Ask your toddler to find the little spikes on the card, then breathe together — in slowly, out slower.

    Ask your child

    "What does the lavender smell like?" "Can you take one slow breath?" "Who visits the lavender — bees or cats?" "Do our hands touch the bees, or watch them?" — answered with a breath, a buzz and hands firmly folded.

    What your child can say or do

    "Lavender!" — often said with a big dramatic sniff. Expect slow breaths offered at bedtime, bees reported on every lavender bush, and the calm-breath trick deployed by your toddler mid-tantrum. That last one is the triumph.

    Out in the real world

    Lavender grows in gardens, parks and tubs by front doors, humming with bees all summer; its smell survives in dried bags and shops. Every purple bush is a breathing station — one slow sniff and pass on.

    Try it together

    Bee counting: stand by a lavender bush and count the bees you can see visiting — one, two, three — quietly, from stillness. Indoors, be bees yourselves: buzz from cushion flower to cushion flower, gentle and slow.

    Understanding check

    At the next big feeling, offer the lavender breath: if a slow sniff-and-blow arrives and the shoulders drop, your toddler owns a calm-down tool for life — the lesson is complete.

    Parent tips

    Practise the breath when nobody needs it, so it is ready when somebody does. Keep bee-watching still and hand-free; bees sting only when grabbed or squashed, and lavender teaches exactly that.

    Staying safe

    Bees are for watching, never touching — and bee-watching happens from a step back so nobody steps on a worker. Lavender itself is safe to smell, but not to eat; and calm-breath practice needs sitting space, not pavement edges.

    This lesson pairs with the Lavender flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Garden Flowers (School Garden).

    LEARNING PATH LESSON · GARDEN FLOWERS · AGES 2 YEARS

    Hibiscus — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

    This lesson goes big: your toddler opens wide like a hibiscus, compares flower-size against face-size, and learns that the grandest blooms keep the shortest running times.

    What is this?

    A hibiscus is a flower of warm places with enormous open petals — pink, red or orange — as wide as a saucer. Each bloom opens wide for a day or two and then folds closed.

    What does it mean?

    The hibiscus is the set’s size card: everything about it says wide, open, enormous. Comparing flower to face is your toddler’s first honest measurement, and big-bigger-biggest is comparison practice in game form.

    What does the child need to know?

    Hibiscus flowers open as wide as a saucer and live in warm, sunny places. Each big bloom only lasts a day or two — the biggest show has the shortest run — and then the flower folds up.

    Why this matters

    Size words need dramatic examples, and wide-as-a-saucer is as dramatic as flowers get. The short bloom also plants a first idea of change over time: big today, folded tomorrow, and that is how flowers work.

    What it teaches

    Size comparison (big, bigger, biggest), arm-stretching whole-body play, warm-climate awareness, day-scale time words (today, tomorrow), and expressive open-wide face-and-body imitation.

    Words to learn

    hibiscusbigwidepetalsopenwarm

    Say this to your child

    “"A hibiscus! Open your arms — thiiis wide! It is the biggest flower on our cards, as wide as a saucer. It lives where it is warm and sunny. Can you be a hibiscus? Open wide... and hold it! And here is a secret: the biggest flowers close up the soonest."”

    Step by step

    1. Show the card, say hibiscus, and open your arms as wide as they will go — this flower is the wide one, and your arms are the petals.
    2. Play big-bigger-biggest: hands small, hands wider, arms widest — three rounds, ending in a full hibiscus star each time.
    3. Compare sizes honestly: is the hibiscus bigger than your face? Hold the card up and let your toddler decide with their own eyes.
    4. Tell the warm-places story: this flower loves the sun and lives where it is hot, which is why it looks like summer itself.
    5. End with the surprise: the biggest bloom in the set closes up after only a day or two — big shows, short runs — then opens fresh on another stem tomorrow.

    Look closer at the picture

    Open your arms wide and say hibiscus into the middle of them. Ask your toddler to find the big petals on the card, then hold the card beside a face — is the flower bigger? Let them measure.

    Ask your child

    "Is the hibiscus big or small?" "Can you open your arms this wide?" "Where does it like to live — warm or cold?" "Which is bigger, the flower or your face?" — answered with an arm-star, a warm word and a face-to-flower measurement.

    What your child can say or do

    "Big one!" Expect arm-star poses at random, hibiscus claims on every large flower, and big-bigger-biggest applied to everything from spoons to dogs. Being measured against a flower is now a legitimate afternoon activity.

    Out in the real world

    Hibiscus blooms in warm gardens and holiday hotels, and stars in books about tropical places; in cooler homes it lives by sunny windows in pots. Every enormous bloom is a rerun of the arm-star.

    Try it together

    Flower measuring: hold the card up against faces, teddies and feet — bigger or smaller? Then lie on the floor and open into hibiscus stars, one at a time, and compare your widest to your widest.

    Understanding check

    Ask which flower on our cards is the biggest: "hibiscus!" with arms opening wide means the size lesson landed — the flower now lives in your toddler’s wingspan.

    Parent tips

    Keep the arm-wide game as your go-to stretch break — it empties wiggles and fills vocabulary at once. If the short-bloom idea puzzles your toddler, act it: open wide, then slowly fold — the flower has finished its show.

    Staying safe

    Big arm movements need big clear space — petals and elbows both knock things over. Real hibiscus blooms are look-only, and any plant from a warm climate stays out of the mouth: look, open wide, hands down.

    This lesson pairs with the Hibiscus flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Garden Flowers (School Garden).

    LEARNING PATH LESSON · GARDEN FLOWERS · AGES 2 YEARS

    Lotus — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

    This lesson floats: your toddler’s hand becomes a lotus on still water, the pond edge becomes a looking place, and the pads on the card become homes a frog might borrow.

    What is this?

    A lotus is a big pink flower that opens on the calm surface of quiet ponds, sitting on wide round pads. It rises out of the muddy water below and opens clean in the morning.

    What does it mean?

    The lotus is the set’s water card, and ponds hold a special spell for toddlers. It also carries a lovely idea to grow into: something beautiful can start in the mud and open clean above it.

    What does the child need to know?

    Lotus flowers float on quiet ponds on big green pads, and frogs like to sit on those pads too. The pond’s edge belongs to grown-ups — we look from the bank with one hand held, and the pond keeps its flowers.

    Why this matters

    Still-water watching slows a toddler down like almost nothing else — ripples, pads, the flower sitting still. And the bank rule is the clearest water-safety boundary the garden set can teach.

    What it teaches

    Gentle floating movements (slow arm-bobs), still-water observation, water-safety boundaries, pond vocabulary (pad, pond, bank), and the patience of watching for a frog that may or may not appear.

    Words to learn

    lotuspondfloatpadwaterstill

    Say this to your child

    “"A lotus! It floats on the quiet pond, on a big green pad. Can you float your hand? Gently... up... down... The lotus grows up out of the muddy water and opens clean and pink. At the pond we hold my hand, stand back from the edge, and look — maybe a frog is sitting on a pad right now."”

    Step by step

    1. Show the card, say lotus, and float your flat hand slowly through the air like a flower on still water — up a little, down a little.
    2. Let your toddler float a hand too, then balance a small toy on the back of their floating hand — a frog on the pad!
    3. Point out the pads on the card: wide, round, flat — that is where a pond frog would sit and watch the day go by.
    4. Tell the muddy secret: the lotus begins deep in the mud under the water and pushes up until it opens clean and pink above it all.
    5. At any real pond, stand back from the edge with one hand held, look for pads and lotus flowers, and whisper so the water stays calm.

    Look closer at the picture

    Float your hand slowly through the air and say lotus. Ask your toddler to find the big round pads on the card, then float together — two flowers on a pond made of living-room air.

    Ask your child

    "Where does the lotus live — on the pond or in the tree?" "What sits on the pads sometimes?" "Can you float your hand?" "Do we run to the pond edge, or hold hands and look?" — answered with floating, a frog noise and a solemn hand-grab.

    What your child can say or do

    "Lotus! Floaty!" Expect hand-floating at bath time, pads claimed on every lily illustration, and frogs suspected on every real pad. The bank rule may be recited back at you at full pond-side volume.

    Out in the real world

    Lotus flowers open on still ponds and in botanical gardens in summer, and lily pads appear on almost every pond in picture books. Each pad seen from the bank is a rerun — float, look, hold the hand, walk on.

    Try it together

    Pond at home: lay a blue blanket as the water, scatter green paper pads, and float toy flowers and frogs on them. Your toddler floats the lotus, hops the frog, and keeps both well away from the blanket’s edge — just like the bank.

    Understanding check

    At the next pond, watch the hands: one reaching for yours before you ask means the water rule is rooted. A floated hand at bath time means the flower is floating too — lesson complete.

    Parent tips

    Bath time is lotus training ground: floating hands, calm water, gentle bobs. Keep the muddy-to-clean story for the two-year-old version — wonder now, meaning later; the picture alone carries it.

    Staying safe

    Pond edges are the real hazard in this lesson: one grown-up hand at all times, no leaning, no reaching for pads or flowers, ever. At home, pond-play blankets are pretend water — real buckets and bowls stay empty and upright.

    This lesson pairs with the Lotus flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Garden Flowers (School Garden).

    LEARNING PATH LESSON · GARDEN FLOWERS · AGES 2 YEARS

    Lily — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

    This lesson stands very still: your toddler becomes a tall lily in a freeze game, curls little fingers back like petals, and practises the grand style of looking without touching.

    What is this?

    A lily is a tall summer flower with petals that curve backwards, and dusty tips called stamens inside. Lilies stand straight in gardens and big bunches at celebrations.

    What does it mean?

    The lily adds a new word-feeling to the set: elegant. Even if the word itself is a stretch for a two-year-old, the pose is not — tall, still, graceful — and pretending elegance is a genuinely funny game.

    What does the child need to know?

    Lilies stand tall with petals that curl back on themselves. We look with hands behind our backs — the dusty dust inside can stain and some lilies are unsafe to chew — so admiring from stillness is the lily way.

    Why this matters

    Hands-behind-back looking is a reusable skill: museums, shops, other people’s gardens. The lily gives it a style and a reason, and the freeze game gives tall-still posture a name your toddler will answer to.

    What it teaches

    Standing stillness on demand, finger-curl fine motor (petals folding back), body posture words (tall, straight, still), and the beginnings of admiring things you do not grab — a social skill in flower form.

    Words to learn

    lilytallpetalscurlstillelegant

    Say this to your child

    “"A lily! Tall and elegant — that means fancy! Stand up straight like a lily... and still... lovely. Its petals curl back, see? Curl your fingers back like petals. And when we see real lilies, we put our hands behind our backs and admire them — that is how fancy flowers get admired."”

    Step by step

    1. Show the card, say lily, and stand up straight and tall — taller than usual, chin up, arms down: a lily at its best.
    2. Hold the still for three slow breaths, then wiggle free and do it again — the freeze game is the lesson’s engine.
    3. Curl your fingers back slowly like petals folding, and let your toddler copy the curl on both hands — tricky, funny, worth it.
    4. Tell the hands-behind-back rule: lilies carry dusty dust inside that we keep off our fingers, so we admire them grandly from stillness.
    5. Finish with a lily parade: stand tall, curl your petals, and process across the room — slow steps, straight backs, maximum elegance.

    Look closer at the picture

    Stand tall and say lily with your chin up. Ask which petals on the card curl backwards, then curl both sets of finger-petals together — slowly, like the flower does.

    Ask your child

    "Is the lily tall or short?" "Which way do its petals curl — back or forward?" "Can you stand still like a lily?" "Where do our hands go when we admire it?" — answered with a freeze, a curl and hands firmly clasped behind.

    What your child can say or do

    "Elegant!" — or a two-year-old version of it. Expect tall-standing freezes in doorways, curled finger-petals waved at dinner, and lilies admired from a dignified distance. Being called elegant will be requested nightly.

    Out in the real world

    Lilies stand in summer gardens, celebration bunches and big shop displays. Every tall white bloom is a rerun — freeze, curl, hands behind backs, one slow admiring walk-past.

    Try it together

    Lily statues: dance to a hum, and when it stops, become lilies — tall, still, fingers curled back. Last lily standing gets to be the breeze that unfreezes everyone else.

    Understanding check

    At the next bunch of flowers, watch the hands: if they drift behind a small back unprompted, the grand style has taken. A freeze on the word lily completes the lesson.

    Parent tips

    Keep the freeze game short and triumph-filled — elegance is exhausting at two. If dust or pollen is visible on real lilies, that is your visible reason: dust stays on the flower, not on fingers.

    Staying safe

    Lily pollen stains and some lilies are toxic if chewed, so hands-off is a real rule, not just style — and keep lily bunches away from cats entirely; they are dangerous to them. Freeze games happen on clear floor, away from stairs.

    This lesson pairs with the Lily flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Garden Flowers (School Garden).

    LEARNING PATH LESSON · GARDEN FLOWERS · AGES 2 YEARS

    Marigold — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

    This lesson rolls along: your toddler winds invisible wool into a marigold ball, collects orange from every corner, and hears about the flower that stands guard next to the vegetables.

    What is this?

    A marigold is a rounded, ruffly flower, often orange, like a tiny pom-pom on a stem. Marigolds bloom for a long time and gardeners set them beside the vegetables — their smell sends some nibbling pests packing.

    What does it mean?

    The marigold is the round card in a set of shapes — a ball, a pom-pom, a winding. And it carries the set’s best job story: a flower with work to do, guarding the vegetable patch with its smell.

    What does the child need to know?

    Marigolds are the orange ball-flowers of the bed, ruffled all over. They have a job: planted beside vegetables, their smell keeps some nibbling pests away — a flower that works for the garden.

    Why this matters

    Round-and-round hand motions are fine-motor practice wrapped in pretend play, and orange needs its champion — the set’s least-practised colour. A working flower rounds out the idea that every plant has a story.

    What it teaches

    Rotating hand movements (winding, rolling), the colour orange in the wild, round-versus-flat shape sorting, and a first helper-story — flowers can have jobs, just like people.

    Words to learn

    marigoldorangeroundruffleballwind

    Say this to your child

    “"A marigold! A whole ball of orange — round and ruffly, like a pom-pom. Can you wind your wool? Round and round... and there is your marigold ball! This flower has a job too: it stands beside the vegetables and its smell keeps the pests away. A working flower!"”

    Step by step

    1. Show the card, say marigold, and roll your hands around each other like winding wool — round and round and round, faster and faster.
    2. Wind an invisible ball together, then hold it up: that is a marigold — a flower shaped like a ball, ruffled from top to bottom.
    3. Ask your toddler to find the round flower on the card and feel the roundness in the air with both hands cupped.
    4. Tell the job story: plant marigolds beside the carrots and their smell keeps the nibblers away — this flower is the garden’s guard.
    5. Take orange hunting on the next outing — leaves, balls, doors, wheelie bins — and cheer every find like the marigold’s own fan club.

    Look closer at the picture

    Circle your hands around each other like winding wool and say marigold into the middle. Ask your toddler to find the round flower on the card, then cup both hands around an invisible ball — the marigold’s shape, held in the air.

    Ask your child

    "Is the marigold round or flat?" "What colour is it?" "Can you wind the wool?" "What job does the marigold do in the garden?" — answered with rolling hands, an "orange!" and a proud guard-story retelling.

    What your child can say or do

    "Ball flower!" Expect hand-winding at every stop, orange collected from pavements to breakfast plates, and marigolds appointed guards of the toy vegetables. The working-flower story will be retold with additions.

    Out in the real world

    Marigolds blaze orange in beds, borders and tubs from spring to autumn, and stand sentry in vegetable patches everywhere. Every pom-pom bloom is a rerun — wind the ball, name the orange, thank the guard.

    Try it together

    Marigold wind-up: wind real wool or ribbon around your toddler’s hands loosely, then unwind into a ball — round, round, round. Finish by coiling it into a bowl: a marigold nest for a toy bee.

    Understanding check

    Ask which flower guards the vegetables: "marigold!" with a winding motion means the story took root. An unprompted "orange!" at the next pumpkin or carrot seals the colour too.

    Parent tips

    Orange is the quietest colour in most homes, so stage a few finds — an orange lid on the table, an orange sock on the line. Keep the winding slow at first; speed comes with the giggles.

    Staying safe

    Garden marigolds are look-and-smell flowers, not snacks — and the soil around vegetable beds is for plants, not fingers. Winding play uses soft ribbon or wool, never string long enough to tangle, and hands stay unwound at the end.

    This lesson pairs with the Marigold flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Garden Flowers (School Garden).

    LEARNING PATH LESSON · GARDEN FLOWERS · AGES 2 YEARS

    Bluebell — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

    This lesson rings softly: your toddler dings pretend bluebells, walks through an imagined blue wood, and learns the gentlest conservation rule a two-year-old can carry.

    What is this?

    Bluebells are small flowers shaped like little bells that grow in woods in spring — so many together that whole carpets of blue appear under the trees.

    What does it mean?

    The bluebell closes the flower set with a whole place: not one bloom but a blue wood. Ringing pretend bells gives the flower a sound, and the wood gives your toddler their first grown-up nature rule.

    What does the child need to know?

    Bluebells look like tiny bells and ring in spring under the trees. They are protected, which means they stay growing where they are — we keep to the path, we pick nothing, and the same blue carpet returns every spring.

    Why this matters

    A rule with a reason — the flowers are protected — is a two-year-old’s first conservation lesson, and it lands kindly: leaving flowers growing is how we make sure they come back. The bell-game makes the leaving feel magical, not missing out.

    What it teaches

    Quiet-to-loud sound play (ding-dong softly, louder only outdoors), make-believe place-building (the blue wood), path-and-boundary awareness, seasonal return thinking, and gentle feet in natural places.

    Words to learn

    bluebellbellsbluewoodsspringpath

    Say this to your child

    “"Bluebells! Little blue bells in the spring woods — ding, dong, so soft. So many of them, they turn the whole wood blue. Our feet keep to the path while every bell stays growing, because the bluebells are protected — and every spring, they all come back to ring for us again."”

    Step by step

    1. Show the card, say bluebell, and flick an imaginary bell with one finger — ding! — soft as a tiny bell really rings.
    2. Ring together, quiet for small bells, a little louder for big ones — then hush and listen: did you hear it ring?
    3. Build the blue wood in the room: walk slowly between cushion trees while your fingers ring bells on every side — blue all around.
    4. Tell the rule with pride, not sternness: bluebells are protected, so they stay in the ground where they grow, and we walk the path like proper wood visitors.
    5. End with the promise: the bells bloom again every spring — same wood, same blue — and one day you will walk through the real carpet together.

    Look closer at the picture

    Flick your finger like ringing a tiny bell and say bluebell. Ask your toddler to find the little bell flowers on the card, then ring bells of your own in the air — quiet dings, close listening.

    Ask your child

    "What do bluebells look like — bells or cups?" "Where do they grow, in the woods or in the bath?" "Do we pick them, or leave them growing?" "What colour is the wood in spring?" — answered with a ding, a blue word and a firm little walk-on.

    What your child can say or do

    "Ding dong!" Expect bell-ringing at every flower, bluebells claimed under every tree, and the path rule recited with woodland gravity. The quiet ding may become your secret signal for soft voices.

    Out in the real world

    Bluebell woods bloom in spring in many places — whole floors of blue under the trees — and they are worth a special trip. Every picture, book or real carpet of blue is a rerun: ring softly, walk the path, wonder.

    Try it together

    Bluebell wood: dim the lights, scatter blue paper or cushions as flowers, and tiptoe the path between them, ringing finger-bells as you go. End with a rest on a log (a cushion) and one soft ding for home.

    Understanding check

    On the next walk through any woods or park, listen for the rule: "we walk on the path" arriving unprompted means the bluebell lesson bloomed. A soft finger-ding at flowers seals it.

    Parent tips

    If you can, visit a real bluebell wood in spring — the card was building to this. Keep the ding quiet indoors and free outdoors; the sound game doubles as a volume dial your toddler can actually find.

    Staying safe

    Bluebells are protected and are not for picking, digging or chewing — bulbs especially stay underground and away from hands. Woods hold stings, ticks and uneven ground: little legs on the path, grown-up eyes on the sky, and hands washed when you get home.

    This lesson pairs with the Bluebell flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Garden Flowers (School Garden).
